definition: Culminate means to reach a final and highest point at the end of a process.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word culminate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know culminate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Years of quiet fundraising culminated in a single afternoon when the library paid off its mortgage and rang the bell on the desk twice.
Build is milder than culminate — excitement or pressure builds long before anything arrives, and building promises nothing about where the rise ends; to culminate is to reach the top at the very end.
Peak stops short of culminate: a season can peak on its middle weekend and keep running, while to culminate is to arrive at the height exactly where the whole run ends.

To climax is to hit the moment of greatest intensity, and the word belongs to drama and feeling — a thriller, a symphony, a shouting match. Culminate makes a cooler, structural claim: a process reaches its highest point exactly where it ends. Intensity is climax's business; shape is culminate's.

To crest is to reach the top and begin easing off — a wave crests, a fever crests, and things keep moving afterward. To culminate is stricter: the height must arrive exactly where the process ends. Cresting can happen anywhere along the way; culminating happens only at the finish.

Latin culmen, the ridgepole at a roof's very top, survives in English only inside culminate and culmination — no everyday cousin shares it. So anchor the meaning to the builder's picture instead: the ridgepole is raised last, and nothing sits above it.
Culminate means to reach a final and highest point at the end of a process.

A stonemason's apprenticeship at the cathedral workshop runs seven years and culminates in the carving of a masterpiece: one block, chosen by the guild, worked without help while the masters watch in silence.
Nothing comes after it but the verdict.
Every earlier year — the sharpening, the lettering, the endless practice moldings — exists to point at that block.
Culminate is exact here because the process reaches its final and highest point at once.
A process that merely stops has ended, not culminated; a process whose best moment came in year three peaked early.
Culminate promises the summit and the finish line are the same place.
Culminate belongs to processes with a shape — campaigns, seasons, apprenticeships — and insists the ending is also the top.
Use peak when the high point may come mid-run, and plain end when there is no height to claim.
Its mirror in this unit is originate: originate names where a line first comes into being; culminate names where it arrives.

The climb itself took nine weeks, but Ines dated the expedition from the day, four years earlier, when she first taped a training schedule to her refrigerator.
Everything in between had an order: gym winters, practice peaks in three countries, a failed attempt that taught her more than the successes.
The expedition culminated on the ridge at dawn on May 9th, when she stood on the summit with nothing above her and nothing left undone.
She distrusted the word at first -- it sounded grand -- until a climbing partner defended it as simple geometry: the highest point, reached last.
Descent began twenty minutes later, but the descent belonged to a different story, the one about getting home.
